sections.readable_text: In [MATH: 1932,] Wiley Post made the first solo flight around the world. Suppose he traveled [MATH: 90] miles in [MATH: 72] minutes. If he maintained this pace, what was his average speed, in miles per hour, to the nearest tenth?

sections.normalized_html:
We're asked to determine the average speed in miles per hour. Therefore, we must first transform the given number of minutes into hours.

There are [MATH: 60\,\textrm{min}] per [MATH: \textrm{h},] which we can write as follows: [MATH: \dfrac{60\,\textrm{min}}{\textrm{h}}]

However, since we're converting from a smaller unit of time [MATH: (\textrm{min})] to a larger one [MATH: (\textrm{h}),] we need to multiply [MATH: 72\,\textrm{min}] by the reciprocal of the above: [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{h}}{60\,\textrm{min}}] This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying [MATH: 72\,\textrm{min}] by our conversion factor, we get [MATH: 72min|= 72min ⋅ (h)/(60min); = 72min ⋅ (h)/(60min); = 72 ⋅ (h)/(60); = (72)/(60)h; = 1.2h.]

Therefore, [MATH: 72\,\textrm{min}] is equivalent to [MATH: 1.2\,\textrm{h}.]

Next, we can use the formula that relates distance, speed, and time: [MATH: \textrm{Speed} = \dfrac{\textrm{Distance}}{\textrm{Time}}]

Substituting the known values ​​in the above formula, we obtain [MATH: Speed|= (90)/(1.2); = 75.0.]

Therefore, the average speed of the flight was [MATH: 75.0] miles per hour.

Which expression represents the time, in seconds, it takes runner [MATH: B] to travel a distance of [MATH: 48q] meters?

sections.normalized_html:
The formula that relates distance, speed, and time is given by [MATH: \text{Speed} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}}.]

Let’s start with runner [MATH: A.] We’re told he travels a distance of [MATH: 8q] meters in time [MATH: t.] So, his speed is [MATH: \text{Speed}_A = \dfrac{8q}{t}.]

Now, we are given that runner [MATH: A] moves at one-fourth the speed of runner [MATH: B.] That means runner [MATH: B] is four times as fast as runner [MATH: A.] So, we have [MATH: Speed_{B}|= 4 ⋅ Speed_{A}; = 4 ⋅ (8q)/(t); = (32q)/(t).]

Finally, we calculate how long it takes runner [MATH: B] to travel [MATH: 48q] meters: [MATH: Time_{B}|= (48q)/((32q/t)); = (48q ⋅ t)/(32q); = (3 ⋅ 16q ⋅ t)/(2 ⋅ 16q); = (3 ⋅ 16q ⋅ t)/(2 ⋅ 16q); = (3t)/(2)]

Therefore, the expression [MATH: \dfrac{3t}{2}] represents the time, in seconds, it takes runner [MATH: B] to travel a distance of [MATH: 48q] meters.
